extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning introductory proof techniques / readers of Richard Hammack's Book of Proof
extracted.subtask_description: Constructing and writing elementary proofs for basic number theory, set theory, divisibility, parity, and induction problems (proof techniques and worked solutions as in Hammack's Book of Proof).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove an implication 'If P then Q', prove the contrapositive 'If not Q then not P' instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples on the page: Problems 11 and 15 use contrapositive proofs. The text explicitly says 'For this we use contrapositive proof.' Often combine with DeMorgan's law when the conclusion is a disjunction (e.g., 'not (a is odd or b is even)' becomes 'a is even and b is odd').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct proof (with case analysis when needed)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the hypothesis and deduce the conclusion directly; when the hypothesis or conclusion is a disjunction, split into cases and prove each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple examples: Problem 11 (converse direction uses direct proof with cases), Problem 13 hint: 'Use direct proof... Then use cases.' The pattern: state 'Suppose ...' then algebraically derive the desired form (often using parity forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume the negation of the desired conclusion and derive a logical impossibility (contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for example in Problem 27 ('(Contradiction) Suppose ... then derive contradiction') and Problem 21 (irrationality proof assumes rational root and gets parity contradiction). Guidance: show some statement (e.g., '0 is odd') which is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express integers by parity (2m or 2m+1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace 'even' by 2m and 'odd' by 2m+1 for integers m to analyze parity of expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widely used across proofs: Problems 11, 15, 27, 29, etc. Example manipulations show expanding (2m+1)^2, grouping terms to exhibit factor 2, or producing '2(...) + 1' to show oddness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove 'if and only if' by proving both directions
rubrics_metrics.description: For P iff Q, prove P->Q and Q->P (the text often uses contrapositive for one direction and direct proof/cases for the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 15 (a + b is even iff a and b have same parity) shows first direction by contrapositive and the converse by cases (both even, both odd).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definition of divisibility (a | b means b = a·k)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving divisibility statements, write the divisibility as an explicit equality and algebraically manipulate to produce the desired factorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Problem 23 (if a|b and a|(b^2−c) then a|c) squares and subtracts to express c as a times integer; Problem 27 and many set-of-multiples manipulations show factoring out the divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Bezout identity / gcd properties
rubrics_metrics.description: When gcd(a,b)=1, use existence of integers x,y with ax+by=1 to derive consequences such as divisibility (e.g., if a|bc then a|c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 29 demonstrates using ax + by = 1 to combine with bc = az and deduce a | c by forming a(cx + zy) = c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear denominators in rational-root arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume a rational root a/b in lowest terms, multiply through by denominator powers to obtain integer equation and analyze parity or divisibility to reach contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in Problem 21: assume rational a/b, clear denominators to get a^3 + ab^2 + 3b^3 = 0 and then analyze parity of terms to contradict 0's parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disprove universal statements by counterexample
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a universal claim is false, provide an explicit counterexample (specific values) that violate the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter 9 contains many disproofs: e.g., show (1) |x+y| = |x|+|y| is false by x=1,y=-1; (3) n^5−n even does not imply n even by n=3, etc. The pattern: pick concrete numbers and compute to demonstrate failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements for integer n by checking base case(s), assuming truth for n=k and showing truth for n=k+1 using algebraic manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many proofs: sums of integers, powers, divisibility (e.g., S = 1+...+n = n^2+n over 2), geometric sum identities, divisibility by 24 of 5^{2n}-1, etc. Explicitly show base case and the algebra transforming k-case to k+1-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When the step may require assuming the statement for all smaller values ≤ k, use strong induction (assume for all ≤ k and prove k+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in arguments such as Fibonacci-sums and some combinatorial proofs; the text explicitly says 'The proof is by strong induction' in relevant problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use algebraic identities and factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply known algebraic factorizations (e.g., x^3−y^3=(x−y)(x^2+xy+y^2)) and expand or regroup polynomials to deduce inequalities or divisibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 23 uses factorization x^3−y^3 to prove monotonicity of cubes; many proofs regroup expanded terms to extract factors of 2 or other integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telescoping sums / partial fraction decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Decompose summands into differences so most terms cancel in the sum (common for 1/(n(n+1)) style sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 15 in Chapter 10 uses the telescoping identity (implicitly or explicitly) 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1) leading to 1 − 1/(n+1). Even when the page presents an inductive proof, the telescoping viewpoint is visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equalities by mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A = B, show A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A by taking an arbitrary element and using definitions of union, intersection, complement, Cartesian product as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many set proofs use this pattern: e.g., proofs that {12n} ⊆ intersection of multiples, A × B ⊆ A × C iff B ⊆ C, distributive laws, etc. The method: assume (x ∈ A) and prove (x ∈ B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply DeMorgan's laws and basic logical equivalences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logical identities (DeMorgan, distributivity, negation laws) to transform set and logical expressions into equivalent forms suitable for proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used heavily in set identity proofs: e.g., A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C) and complement manipulations where the text explicitly invokes DeMorgan and regrouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'without loss of generality' to reduce symmetric cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When two cases are symmetric, assume one (e.g., 'Let a be even and b odd') to avoid repeating nearly identical arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 15 uses 'Without loss of generality, let's say that a is even and b is odd' when proving the contrapositive. Guidance: only do this when symmetry justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive existence proofs (give explicit example)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove existence, exhibit a specific object that satisfies the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Problem 17 ('There is a prime between 90 and 100') solved by observing 97 is prime. Many other elementary existence claims are handled by construction or exhibited values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by removal and re-addition (incremental induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For counting problems, remove an element to apply the induction hypothesis, then add it back and count the additional contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the plane regions problem: remove one line, apply formula for n lines, then add back the (n+1)th line and count the n+1 new regions it creates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pascal's identity and binomial coefficient identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply Pascal's formula and combinatorial identities when proving binomial theorem, sums of binomial coefficients, or combinatorial equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems 23 (binomial theorem via induction) and 31 (sum of binomial coefficients identity) explicitly use Pascal's identity in the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show gcd conclusions by considering common divisors and differences
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove gcd(n,n+1)=1, let d divide both and show d divides their difference (1) so d=±1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem 31 uses this standard Euclidean-difference argument; similarly gcd(2n+1,4n^2+1)=1 is handled by expressing one quantity as a multiple plus remainder 2 and arguing divisors must be 1 or 2 and are odd, hence 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label / state proof technique at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly name the chosen proof method (e.g., 'Direct', 'Contradiction', 'Contrapositive', 'Induction') at the start of the proof to clarify approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout the page the author begins proofs with labels like 'Proof. (Direct)', 'Proof. (Contradiction)', or 'Proof. (Outline)'. This helps readers follow structure and signals strategy.
